topic: Phone and CW operating (G2A, G2C; 23 pool questions)

notes.front: What is VOX?
notes.back: Voice-operated transmit switching: the transceiver switches to transmit automatically when it detects your voice.
notes.explanation: It frees both hands, unlike a push-to-talk switch that must be held or pressed.
notes.example: Talking into the microphone with no button pressed and having the rig switch to transmit on its own.

notes.front: What does calling “CQ DX” mean?
notes.back: A general call inviting contacts from outside your own country or region, not from nearby stations.
notes.explanation: It tells nearby stations not to answer, saving time for the distant contact the caller wants.
notes.example: A US station in the lower 48 calling “CQ DX” is inviting replies from outside the lower 48 states.

notes.front: What does automatic level control (ALC) do?
notes.back: It limits transmitter drive to prevent overdriving the final amplifier and distorting the signal.
notes.explanation: Without it, excess audio or mic gain would push the transmitter into distortion and splatter.
notes.example: Turning up the mic gain too far triggers the ALC meter to show it is now limiting the drive.

notes.front: What is full break-in (QSK)?
notes.back: A CW operating mode where the receiver opens between individual code elements, so you can hear between dits and dahs while sending.
notes.explanation: It lets an operator catch an interrupting call almost instantly, unlike switching manually between transmit and receive.
notes.example: Hearing another station break in mid-word because your receiver reopens in the gaps between your own dots and dashes.

notes.front: What does the CW prosign “KN” mean?
notes.back: Listening only for a specific station or stations to reply.
notes.explanation: It tells other stations not to break in, unlike a general invitation to any caller.
notes.example: Ending a transmission with “KN” when you only want the station you are already working to come back.

notes.front: What does the CW prosign “AR” mean?
notes.back: The end of a formal message.
notes.explanation: It tells the receiving station the formal message is complete, distinct from “KN” which restricts who may answer.
notes.example: Sending “AR” after finishing a formal traffic message on CW.

notes.front: What does the Q signal “QRS?” ask?
notes.back: QRS means “send slower”; if a station sends “QRS?”, slow down.
notes.explanation: It is a quick way to ask for a slower sending speed without switching to voice.
notes.example: A learner sends “QRS” to a fast CW operator to ask them to slow down.

notes.front: What does the Q signal “QRL?” ask?
notes.back: “Are you busy?” or “Is this frequency in use?”
notes.explanation: Sending it before calling CQ checks that you are not about to interfere with an ongoing contact.
notes.example: Sending “QRL?” on an apparently clear CW frequency before calling CQ.

notes.front: What does the Q signal “QSL” mean?
notes.back: “I have received and understood.”
notes.explanation: It confirms a message got through, distinct from a general acknowledgement of prior contact.
notes.example: Sending “QSL” to confirm you copied a station's report correctly.

notes.front: What does the Q signal “QRN” mean?
notes.back: “I am troubled by static.”
notes.explanation: It flags an atmospheric-noise problem, distinct from man-made interference.
notes.example: Sending “QRN” during a thunderstorm-heavy summer evening when static crashes are obscuring the signal.

notes.front: What does the Q signal “QRV” mean?
notes.back: “I am ready to receive.”
notes.explanation: It signals you are prepared for the other station to send.
notes.example: Answering “QRV” when asked if you are ready to copy a message.

notes.front: What does “zero beat” mean in CW operation?
notes.back: Matching your transmit frequency exactly to the frequency of a received signal.
notes.explanation: It avoids an audible offset (beat note) between two stations, keeping the contact on the same frequency.
notes.example: Tuning until your sidetone and the received tone match in pitch, so you transmit on the other station's frequency.

notes.front: What is an RST report?
notes.back: The CW signal report to which a "C" can be added, to flag a chirpy or unstable signal.
notes.explanation: It is the standard shorthand way CW operators describe how well a signal is being received.
notes.example: Adding "C" to an RST report tells the other station their signal sounds chirpy or unstable.

notes.front: What is a signal report?
notes.back: A quick assessment of how well a station's signal is being received, exchanged near the start of a contact.
notes.explanation: It tells the other operator how to adjust, or whether the path supports the contact at all.
notes.example: Voice operators exchange a report like “five nine” instead of the CW RST code.

notes.front: Which sideband is normally used for voice above 14 MHz, including 17 and 12 m and VHF/UHF SSB?
notes.back: Upper sideband (USB).
notes.explanation: This is accepted practice, not a Part 97 requirement.
notes.source: NCVEC 2023–2027 General Pool, G2A01, G2A03, G2A04

notes.front: Which sideband is normally used for voice on 160, 75 and 40 m?
notes.back: Lower sideband (LSB).
notes.explanation: 97.301(d) does not mandate this; it is commonly accepted amateur practice.

notes.front: What is SSB's main advantage over other analog HF voice modes?
notes.back: Less bandwidth and greater power efficiency.
notes.explanation: Removing the carrier and one sideband concentrates power into the information that is actually sent.

notes.front: In SSB, what exactly is transmitted?
notes.back: Only one sideband; the other sideband and the carrier are suppressed.
notes.explanation: This distinguishes true SSB from AM, which sends both sidebands and the carrier.

notes.front: What is the recommended way to break into a phone contact?
notes.back: Say your call sign once.
notes.explanation: A single, clear call sign is enough; anything more is unnecessary and can be disruptive.

notes.front: What is the main benefit of VOX over PTT operation?
notes.back: It allows hands-free operation.
notes.explanation: The transceiver switches to transmit on voice alone, freeing the operator's hands for other tasks.

notes.front: Who should normally respond to a US station in the contiguous 48 states calling “CQ DX”?
notes.back: Any station outside the lower 48 states.
notes.explanation: The call specifically seeks distant contacts, not nearby domestic ones.

notes.front: What control is typically adjusted for proper ALC setting on an SSB transceiver?
notes.back: Transmit audio or microphone gain.
notes.explanation: Reducing the drive at its source, rather than at the RF output, is how ALC is normally set correctly.

notes.front: What happens during full break-in (QSK) CW operation?
notes.back: The transmitting station can receive between individual code characters and elements.
notes.explanation: This differs from ordinary CW operation, which switches transmit/receive only between whole transmissions.

notes.front: What does a “C” added to an RST report mean?
notes.back: A chirpy or unstable signal.
notes.explanation: It is an extension operators add to the standard RST code to flag a specific transmitter fault.

notes.front: What is the best speed to use when answering a CQ in Morse code?
notes.back: The fastest speed you are comfortable copying, but no faster than the CQ.
notes.explanation: Matching or staying below the caller's speed keeps the exchange within both operators' comfort.

notes.front: Why do most amateur stations use lower sideband on 160, 75 and 40 m?
notes.back: It is commonly accepted amateur practice.
notes.explanation: No rule mandates it; it is a long-standing convention, not a licence requirement.

notes.front: Which sideband is normally used for SSB voice on VHF and UHF?
notes.back: Upper sideband (USB).
notes.explanation: This follows the same convention as HF above 14 MHz.

notes.front: Which mode is most commonly used for voice communications on frequencies of 14 MHz or higher?
notes.back: Upper sideband
notes.choices:
A) Upper sideband
B) Lower sideband
C) Suppressed sideband
D) Double sideband
notes.choicesExplained: B: LSB is the convention on 160, 75 and 40 m. C: “Suppressed sideband” is not a distinct mode name here. D: double sideband is not the accepted voice convention.
notes.explanation: Upper sideband is accepted practice at 14 MHz and above.

notes.front: Which mode is most commonly used for voice communications on the 160-, 75-, and 40-meter bands?
notes.back: Lower sideband
notes.choices:
A) Upper sideband
B) Lower sideband
C) Suppressed sideband
D) Double sideband
notes.choicesExplained: A: USB is the convention at 14 MHz and above. C: not a distinct mode name here. D: not the accepted voice convention.
notes.explanation: LSB is accepted practice on these lower HF bands.

notes.front: Which mode is most commonly used for SSB voice communications in the VHF and UHF bands?
notes.back: Upper sideband
notes.choices:
A) Upper sideband
B) Lower sideband
C) Suppressed sideband
D) Double sideband
notes.choicesExplained: B: LSB is the convention on the lower HF bands, not VHF/UHF. C: not a distinct mode name here. D: not the accepted voice convention.
notes.explanation: USB is the VHF/UHF SSB voice convention, matching the 14 MHz and up HF convention.

notes.front: Which mode is most commonly used for voice communications on the 17- and 12-meter bands?
notes.back: Upper sideband
notes.choices:
A) Upper sideband
B) Lower sideband
C) Suppressed sideband
D) Double sideband
notes.choicesExplained: B: LSB is used on the lower bands, not 17/12 m. C: not a distinct mode name here. D: not the accepted voice convention.
notes.explanation: 17 and 12 m follow the same USB convention as 14 MHz and above.

notes.front: Which mode of voice communication is most commonly used on the HF amateur bands?
notes.back: Single sideband
notes.choices:
A) Frequency modulation
B) Double sideband
C) Single sideband
D) Single phase modulation
notes.choicesExplained: A: FM is mainly a VHF/UHF mode. B: double sideband is not the common HF voice mode. D: not a real HF voice mode name.
notes.explanation: SSB is the dominant HF voice mode for its bandwidth and efficiency.

notes.front: Which of the following is an advantage of using single sideband, as compared to other analog voice modes on the HF amateur bands?
notes.back: Less bandwidth used and greater power efficiency
notes.choices:
A) Very high-fidelity voice modulation
B) Less subject to interference from atmospheric static crashes
C) Ease of tuning on receive and immunity to impulse noise
D) Less bandwidth used and greater power efficiency
notes.choicesExplained: A: SSB trades some fidelity for efficiency, it is not the high-fidelity choice. B: SSB is not specifically immune to static crashes. C: SSB is actually harder to tune on receive than AM or FM.
notes.explanation: SSB's advantage is narrower bandwidth and better use of transmitter power, not fidelity or noise immunity.

notes.front: Which of the following statements is true of single sideband (SSB)?
notes.back: Only one sideband is transmitted; the other sideband and carrier are suppressed
notes.choices:
A) Only one sideband and the carrier are transmitted; the other sideband is suppressed
B) Only one sideband is transmitted; the other sideband and carrier are suppressed
C) SSB is the only voice mode authorized on the 20-, 15-, and 10-meter amateur bands
D) SSB is the only voice mode authorized on the 160-, 75-, and 40-meter amateur bands
notes.choicesExplained: A: in SSB the carrier is suppressed too. C: other voice modes are not barred from those bands by rule. D: other voice modes are not barred from those bands by rule.
notes.explanation: True SSB suppresses both the carrier and the unused sideband.

notes.front: What is the recommended way to break into a phone contact?
notes.back: Say your call sign once
notes.choices:
A) Say “QRZ” several times, followed by your call sign
B) Say your call sign once
C) Say “Breaker Breaker”
D) Say “CQ” followed by the call sign of either station
notes.choicesExplained: A: repeating “QRZ” is unnecessary and not the recommended method. C: that is CB slang, not accepted amateur practice. D: calling CQ is for starting a new contact, not breaking into one.
notes.explanation: A single call sign is the accepted, minimally disruptive way to break in.

notes.front: Why do most amateur stations use lower sideband on the 160-, 75-, and 40-meter bands?
notes.back: It is commonly accepted amateur practice
notes.choices:
A) Lower sideband is more efficient than upper sideband at these frequencies
B) Lower sideband is the only sideband legal on these frequency bands
C) Because it is fully compatible with an AM detector
D) It is commonly accepted amateur practice
notes.choicesExplained: A: there is no efficiency difference between LSB and USB. B: no rule restricts these bands to LSB only. C: SSB is not designed for compatibility with an AM detector.
notes.explanation: There is no technical or legal reason; it is simply the accepted convention.

notes.front: Which of the following statements is true of VOX operation versus PTT operation?
notes.back: It allows “hands free” operation
notes.choices:
A) The received signal is more natural sounding
B) It allows “hands free” operation
C) It occupies less bandwidth
D) It provides more power output
notes.choicesExplained: A: VOX does not change how natural the received audio sounds. C: VOX does not change occupied bandwidth. D: VOX does not change transmitter power output.
notes.explanation: VOX's defining benefit is hands-free switching, not audio quality, bandwidth or power.

notes.front: Generally, who should respond to a station in the contiguous 48 states calling “CQ DX”?
notes.back: Any stations outside the lower 48 states
notes.choices:
A) Any caller is welcome to respond
B) Only stations in Germany
C) Any stations outside the lower 48 states
D) Only contest stations
notes.choicesExplained: A: nearby domestic stations should not answer a DX call. B: the call is not limited to any single country. D: the call is not limited to contest operation.
notes.explanation: “CQ DX” specifically invites replies from outside the lower 48 states.

notes.front: What control is typically adjusted for proper ALC setting on a single sideband transceiver?
notes.back: Transmit audio or microphone gain
notes.choices:
A) RF clipping level
B) Transmit audio or microphone gain
C) Antenna inductance or capacitance
D) Attenuator level
notes.choicesExplained: A: clipping level is a processor setting, not the drive control that sets ALC. C: antenna matching does not set ALC. D: a receive attenuator does not affect transmit ALC.
notes.explanation: Reducing drive at the audio/mic gain stage is the normal way to set ALC correctly.

notes.front: Which of the following describes full break-in CW operation (QSK)?
notes.back: Transmitting stations can receive between code characters and elements
notes.choices:
A) Breaking stations send the Morse code prosign “BK”
B) Automatic keyers, instead of hand keys, are used to send Morse code
C) An operator must activate a manual send/receive switch before and after every transmission
D) Transmitting stations can receive between code characters and elements
notes.choicesExplained: A: the “BK” prosign is unrelated to defining QSK. B: keyer type does not define full break-in. C: a manual switch is the opposite of full break-in, which needs no manual switching.
notes.explanation: QSK lets the receiver open in the gaps between elements of the transmitted code.

notes.front: What should you do if a CW station sends “QRS?”
notes.back: Send slower
notes.choices:
A) Send slower
B) Change frequency
C) Increase your power
D) Repeat everything twice
notes.choicesExplained: B: QRS is not a request to change frequency. C: QRS is not a request about power. D: QRS is not a request to repeat.
notes.explanation: QRS asks for a slower sending speed.

notes.front: What does it mean when a CW operator sends “KN” at the end of a transmission?
notes.back: Listening only for a specific station or stations
notes.choices:
A) No US stations should call
B) Operating full break-in
C) Listening only for a specific station or stations
D) Closing station now
notes.choicesExplained: A: KN says nothing about US stations specifically. B: KN does not indicate break-in mode. D: KN does not mean the station is closing down.
notes.explanation: KN restricts replies to the specific station or stations already in contact.

notes.front: What does the Q signal “QRL?” mean?
notes.back: “Are you busy?” or “Is this frequency in use?”
notes.choices:
A) “Will you keep the frequency clear?”
B) “Are you operating full break-in?” or “Can you operate full break-in?”
C) “Are you listening only for a specific station?”
D) “Are you busy?” or “Is this frequency in use?”
notes.choicesExplained: A: that is not what QRL? asks. B: QSK, not QRL, concerns full break-in. C: KN, not QRL, concerns listening for a specific station.
notes.explanation: QRL? asks whether the frequency is already occupied.

notes.front: What is the best speed to use when answering a CQ in Morse code?
notes.back: The fastest speed at which you are comfortable copying, but no faster than the CQ
notes.choices:
A) The fastest speed at which you are comfortable copying, but no slower than the CQ
B) The fastest speed at which you are comfortable copying, but no faster than the CQ
C) At the standard calling speed of 10 wpm
D) At the standard calling speed of 5 wpm
notes.choicesExplained: A: there is no rule requiring a minimum speed; matching the CQ's pace is the guide. C: there is no fixed “standard” 10 wpm answering speed. D: there is no fixed “standard” 5 wpm answering speed.
notes.explanation: Match your comfortable copying speed, capped at the CQ caller's own speed.

notes.front: What does the term “zero beat” mean in CW operation?
notes.back: Matching the transmit frequency to the frequency of a received signal
notes.choices:
A) Matching the speed of the transmitting station
B) Operating split to avoid interference on frequency
C) Sending without error
D) Matching the transmit frequency to the frequency of a received signal
notes.choicesExplained: A: zero beat concerns frequency, not sending speed. B: split operation is a different technique. C: zero beat has nothing to do with sending accuracy.
notes.explanation: Zero beat means tuning your transmit frequency to exactly match the received signal.

notes.front: When sending CW, what does a “C” mean when added to the RST report?
notes.back: Chirpy or unstable signal
notes.choices:
A) Chirpy or unstable signal
B) Report was read from an S meter rather than estimated
C) 100 percent copy
D) Key clicks
notes.choicesExplained: B: an S-meter-based report is not what the added C indicates. C: 100 percent copy is not what the added C indicates. D: key clicks are a separate, unrelated fault.
notes.explanation: The added “C” flags a chirpy, unstable note.

notes.front: What prosign is sent to indicate the end of a formal message when using CW?
notes.back: AR
notes.choices:
A) SK
B) BK
C) AR
D) KN
notes.choicesExplained: A: SK marks the end of a contact, not a formal message specifically. B: BK is used for breaking in, not ending a formal message. D: KN restricts who may reply, it does not end a formal message.
notes.explanation: AR marks the end of a formal message.

notes.front: What does the Q signal “QSL” mean?
notes.back: I have received and understood
notes.choices:
A) Send slower
B) We have already confirmed the contact
C) I have received and understood
D) We have worked before
notes.choicesExplained: A: QRS, not QSL, asks for slower sending. B: QSL is the act of confirming, not a statement that confirmation already happened. D: QSL does not indicate a prior contact.
notes.explanation: QSL confirms the message was received and understood.

notes.front: What does the Q signal “QRN” mean?
notes.back: I am troubled by static
notes.choices:
A) Send more slowly
B) Stop sending
C) Zero beat my signal
D) I am troubled by static
notes.choicesExplained: A: QRS, not QRN, asks for slower sending. B: QRN is not a stop-sending instruction. C: QRN has nothing to do with zero beating.
notes.explanation: QRN reports being bothered by atmospheric static.

notes.front: What does the Q signal “QRV” mean?
notes.back: I am ready to receive
notes.choices:
A) You are sending too fast
B) There is interference on the frequency
C) I am quitting for the day
D) I am ready to receive
notes.choicesExplained: A: QRV does not comment on sending speed. B: interference is not what QRV means; QRV = ready to receive. C: QRV does not mean signing off for the day.
notes.explanation: QRV reports readiness to receive.

notes.front: Where is USB conventionally used, and where is LSB conventionally used?
notes.back: USB: 14 MHz and above (20, 17, 15, 12, 10 m, VHF/UHF SSB). LSB: 160, 75 and 40 m.
notes.explanation: Both are accepted practice, not a Part 97 rule, but mismatching sidebands confuses other operators.

notes.front: What is the difference between the CW prosigns KN and AR?
notes.back: KN restricts replies to a specific station; AR marks the end of a formal message and says nothing about who may reply.
notes.explanation: One controls who may answer next; the other simply closes out a message.

notes.front: How do QRL?, QRS, QRV and QRN differ?
notes.back: QRL? asks if the frequency is busy; QRS asks to slow down; QRV means ready to receive; QRN reports static.
notes.explanation: Each Q signal answers a different operating question, so mixing them up sends the wrong message.
notes.source: NCVEC 2023–2027 General Pool, G2C02, G2C04, G2C10, G2C11
